The Python version of the code slides and the in-class exercise of the logistic regression deck, with the packages of the course: polars, great_tables, statsmodels and plotnine. The data are simulated for a mobile operator (`data/churn/telco_churn.csv`, made by `data/generate_churn_data.py`, seed 33): 11,000 customers in Germany, Austria, Spain and Poland, and whether they cancelled within the next 12 months (churn). The true effects of the drivers are the same in every country, but the countries differ in their baseline churn, in the amount of unexplained variation (the scale) and in how customers use the satisfaction scale (response styles). The retention offer was randomised: a pilot in which half of the customers were picked at random.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `customer_id` | customer number |
| `country` | DE, AT, ES or PL |
| `age` | age in years |
| `tenure_months` | months as a customer |
| `monthly` | 1 = month-to-month contract, 0 = 24-month contract |
| `monthly_fee` | monthly fee in EUR |
| `price_increase` | 1 = price rise in the last six months |
| `complaints` | calls to the complaints line in the last six months |
| `satisfaction` | survey score, 1 to 5 |
| `retention_offer` | 1 = randomly picked for the pilot retention offer |
| `churn` | 1 = left within the next 12 months |

This file sits in `sessions/01-foundations/`, so it reads the data two folders up (`../../data/...`). Every number on the slides of the deck is printed somewhere below.

## Step 0: load and look

```{python}
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from great_tables import GT
from plotnine import (aes, element_text, facet_wrap, geom_abline, geom_col, geom_errorbar,
                      geom_hline, geom_line, geom_point, geom_ribbon, ggplot, labs,
                      position_dodge, scale_color_manual, scale_fill_manual, scale_x_continuous,
                      scale_x_discrete, scale_y_continuous, theme, theme_minimal)

churn = pl.read_csv("../../data/churn/telco_churn.csv")
df = churn.to_pandas()

FORMULA = "churn ~ monthly + price_increase + complaints + np.log(tenure_months)"
COUNTRIES = ["DE", "AT", "ES", "PL"]
COLOURS = {"DE": "#002350", "AT": "#8C8C8C", "ES": "#0096D3", "PL": "#7FB800"}
percent = lambda v: [f"{x:.0%}" for x in v]          # axis labels in %

overview = (churn.group_by("country", maintain_order=True)      # keeps the order DE, AT, ES, PL
            .agg(pl.len().alias("customers"),
                 pl.col("churn").mean().alias("churn_rate"),
                 pl.col("monthly").mean().alias("share_month_to_month"),
                 pl.col("satisfaction").mean().alias("mean_satisfaction"),
                 pl.col("churn").filter(pl.col("monthly") == 1).mean()
                 .alias("churn_month_to_month"),
                 pl.col("churn").filter(pl.col("monthly") == 0).mean().alias("churn_24_month")))
(GT(overview)
 .fmt_integer(columns="customers")
 .fmt_percent(columns=["churn_rate", "share_month_to_month", "churn_month_to_month",
                       "churn_24_month"], decimals=1)
 .fmt_number(columns="mean_satisfaction", decimals=2)
 .tab_header(title="Customers by country", subtitle="Simulated data: telco_churn.csv"))
```

Spanish (34.7 %) and Polish (28.5 %) customers churn about twice as often as German (15.4 %) and Austrian (14.6 %) ones, and in every country month-to-month customers churn far more often than customers on a 24-month contract. Spanish customers also give higher satisfaction scores (3.35 vs 2.96 in Germany), although they churn more: keep that in mind for Step 5.

How to read it: the baselines differ a lot between the countries, and the baseline decides how many percentage points a coefficient is worth.

## Step 1: odds, odds ratio and log-odds by hand

The calculator examples of the slides, with invented round counts (not the data): in Germany 50 of 100 month-to-month customers and 20 of 100 customers on a 24-month contract churn; in Spain 60 of 100 and 30 of 100. The function below takes counts by country and contract and returns the probability, the odds and the log-odds, and then the ratios of month-to-month vs 24-month.

```{python}
def odds_table(counts):
    """p, odds and log-odds by country and contract, and month-to-month vs 24-month."""
    long = (counts.with_columns(p=pl.col("churners") / pl.col("customers"))
            .with_columns(odds=pl.col("p") / (1 - pl.col("p")))
            .with_columns(log_odds=pl.col("odds").log()))
    wide = long.pivot(on="monthly", index="country", values=["p", "odds", "log_odds"])
    ratios = wide.select("country",
                         ((pl.col("p_1") - pl.col("p_0")) * 100).alias("gap_pp"),
                         (pl.col("p_1") / pl.col("p_0")).alias("risk_ratio"),
                         (pl.col("odds_1") / pl.col("odds_0")).alias("odds_ratio"),
                         (pl.col("log_odds_1") - pl.col("log_odds_0")).alias("log_odds_diff"))
    return long, ratios


calculator = pl.DataFrame({"country": ["DE", "DE", "ES", "ES"], "monthly": [1, 0, 1, 0],
                           "customers": [100, 100, 100, 100], "churners": [50, 20, 60, 30]})
long, ratios = odds_table(calculator)
GT(long).fmt_number(columns=["p", "odds"], decimals=4).fmt_number(columns="log_odds", decimals=3) \
    .tab_header(title="Calculator example: invented counts", subtitle="monthly = 1: month-to-month")
```

```{python}
GT(ratios).fmt_number(columns=["gap_pp"], decimals=1) \
    .fmt_number(columns=["risk_ratio", "odds_ratio"], decimals=2) \
    .fmt_number(columns="log_odds_diff", decimals=3) \
    .tab_header(title="Month-to-month vs 24-month: invented counts")
```

Both countries have the same gap of 30 percentage points (pp), but different odds ratios (4.0 in Germany, 3.5 in Spain) and risk ratios (2.5 and 2.0). The difference of the log-odds (1.386 and 1.253) is the log of the odds ratio. A logit with `monthly` alone returns exactly these numbers: the intercept is the log-odds of the 24-month customers, the coefficient the difference of the log-odds. To check, we build the 200 customers of each country from the counts.

```{python}
def from_counts(churners_monthly, churners_24_month, n=100):
    """n month-to-month and n 24-month customers with the given numbers of churners."""
    return pl.DataFrame({
        "monthly": [1] * n + [0] * n,
        "churn": ([1] * churners_monthly + [0] * (n - churners_monthly)
                  + [1] * churners_24_month + [0] * (n - churners_24_month))}).to_pandas()


de = from_counts(50, 20)
es = from_counts(60, 30)
smf.logit("churn ~ monthly", data=es).fit().params
```

```{python}
smf.logit("churn ~ monthly", data=de).fit().params
```

`.fit()` prints a short message on the optimisation; `.fit(disp=0)` silences it, which we do from now on. The same table for the real data of Germany and Spain:

```{python}
real_counts = (churn.filter(pl.col("country").is_in(["DE", "ES"]))
               .group_by("country", "monthly")
               .agg(pl.len().alias("customers"), pl.col("churn").sum().alias("churners"))
               .sort("country", "monthly", descending=[False, True]))
real_long, real_ratios = odds_table(real_counts)
GT(real_long).fmt_percent(columns="p", decimals=1) \
    .fmt_number(columns=["odds", "log_odds"], decimals=3) \
    .tab_header(title="Real data: Germany and Spain", subtitle="Simulated data: telco_churn.csv")
```

```{python}
GT(real_ratios).fmt_number(columns="gap_pp", decimals=1) \
    .fmt_number(columns=["risk_ratio", "odds_ratio", "log_odds_diff"], decimals=2)
```

How to read it: in the data, month-to-month customers churn at 26.4 % vs 9.6 % in Germany and at 46.6 % vs 24.7 % in Spain; the odds ratio is larger in Germany, the gap in percentage points larger in Spain, so the two measures can rank the countries differently.

## Step 2: pooled logit with country dummies

One model for all four countries with country dummies (Germany as reference). We first define a helper for average marginal effects by group (Step 3 uses it): predict every customer twice, once with `var` set to 1 and once with 0, and average the difference within each country. It is the Python version of `avg_comparisons(..., by = "country")` in R's marginaleffects.

```{python}
def ame(model, data, var, by="country"):
    """Average change in the churn probability from var = 0 to var = 1, by group."""
    change = model.predict(data.assign(**{var: 1})) - model.predict(data.assign(**{var: 0}))
    return change.groupby(data[by]).mean()
```

The model of slide 36. `smf.logit` works like `smf.ols`; the coefficients are on the log-odds scale.

```{python}
m = smf.logit(
    "churn ~ monthly + price_increase"
    " + complaints + np.log(tenure_months)"
    " + C(country, Treatment('DE'))",
    data=df).fit()
```

Coefficients, odds ratios (`exp(b)`) and p-values in one table. `print(m.summary())` gives the full statsmodels table with standard errors.

```{python}
coefs = pl.DataFrame({"term": m.params.index.to_list(), "coefficient": m.params.to_list(),
                      "odds_ratio": np.exp(m.params).to_list(),
                      "p": ["< 0.001" if v < 0.001 else f"{v:.3f}" for v in m.pvalues]})
(GT(coefs)
 .fmt_number(columns="coefficient", decimals=3)
 .fmt_number(columns="odds_ratio", decimals=2)
 .tab_header(title="Pooled churn logit with country dummies", subtitle="Reference: Germany")
 .tab_source_note(f"McFadden pseudo-R²: {m.prsquared:.3f}; n = {int(m.nobs):,}"))
```

The odds ratio of `np.log(tenure_months)` refers to a change of one in the log of tenure, which is hard to read. Doubling tenure raises the log by ln 2, so it multiplies the odds by 2 to the power of the coefficient:

```{python}
b_tenure = m.params["np.log(tenure_months)"]
print(f"doubling tenure multiplies the odds of churn by {2 ** b_tenure:.2f}")
```

How to read it: a month-to-month contract multiplies the odds of churn by 2.62, each complaint call by 1.57 and a price rise by 1.83; Spain's 2.88 and Poland's 1.86 are differences in the baseline, not drivers, and Austria does not differ from Germany (p = 0.907).

## Step 3: average marginal effects by country

`get_margeff()` gives the average marginal effects (AMEs): the average change in the churn probability. `dummy=True` treats the 0/1 variables (`monthly`, `price_increase`) as switches from 0 to 1 instead of slopes.

```{python}
m.get_margeff(dummy=True).summary()
```

The AME of the month-to-month contract by country, with the helper of Step 2:

```{python}
ame(m, df, "monthly")    # by country
```

The same in percentage points, next to each country's churn rate:

```{python}
ame_pooled = ame(m, df, "monthly")
ame_table = overview.select("country", "churn_rate").with_columns(
    ame_monthly_pp=pl.Series([100 * ame_pooled[country] for country in COUNTRIES]))
GT(ame_table).fmt_percent(columns="churn_rate", decimals=1) \
    .fmt_number(columns="ame_monthly_pp", decimals=2) \
    .tab_header(title="Month-to-month contract: AME by country", subtitle="Pooled model of Step 2")
```

The pooled model has one coefficient for the contract (0.962), the same in all four countries. Its AME still differs: 12.40 pp in Germany, 12.29 pp in Austria, 20.11 pp in Spain and 17.31 pp in Poland, because the same change in log-odds moves the probability more when the baseline is closer to 50 %, where the S-curve is steep.

How to read it: report the effect of a driver in percentage points by country, not as one coefficient; with different baselines one coefficient means different effects. But the pooled model forces one slope on all countries, and with different logit scales that overstates the gap between countries (here 12.4 vs 20.1 pp; the true effects, from a large simulation, are about 16.7 and 17.6 pp). For a comparison, use country-specific slopes: separate logits (Step 4) or the interaction model (Step 6).

## Step 4: separate country logits: the warm-up

One logit per country, with the churn formula. The AME of `monthly` is the first entry of `margeff`.

```{python}
rows = []
for country in COUNTRIES:
    part = df[df["country"] == country]
    m_c = smf.logit(FORMULA, data=part).fit(disp=0)
    rows.append({"country": country, "coef_monthly": m_c.params["monthly"],
                 "odds_ratio": np.exp(m_c.params["monthly"]),
                 "ame_monthly_pp": 100 * m_c.get_margeff(at="overall", dummy=True).margeff[0],
                 "churn_rate": part["churn"].mean()})
flip = pl.DataFrame(rows).with_columns(
    rank_coef=pl.col("coef_monthly").rank(descending=True).cast(pl.Int64),
    rank_ame=pl.col("ame_monthly_pp").rank(descending=True).cast(pl.Int64))
(GT(flip)
 .fmt_number(columns="coef_monthly", decimals=3)
 .fmt_number(columns=["odds_ratio", "ame_monthly_pp"], decimals=2)
 .fmt_percent(columns="churn_rate", decimals=1)
 .tab_header(title="Month-to-month contract: coefficient vs AME",
             subtitle="Separate country logits"))
```

```{python}
flip_long = (flip.unpivot(index="country", on=["coef_monthly", "ame_monthly_pp"],
                          variable_name="measure", value_name="value")
             .with_columns(pl.col("measure").replace({"coef_monthly": "Coefficient (log-odds)",
                                                      "ame_monthly_pp": "AME (pp)"})
                          .cast(pl.Enum(["Coefficient (log-odds)", "AME (pp)"]))))
(ggplot(flip_long.to_pandas(), aes("country", "value", fill="country"))
 + geom_col(width=0.7)
 + facet_wrap("~measure", scales="free_y")
 + scale_x_discrete(limits=COUNTRIES)
 + scale_fill_manual(values=COLOURS, guide=None)
 + labs(x="", y="")
 + theme_minimal()
 + theme(figure_size=(8, 3.5)))
```

Is the Germany–Spain gap larger than sampling error? A z test for the difference of two independent estimates, once for the coefficients and once for the AMEs (standard errors from `bse` and `margeff_se`):

```{python}
est = {}
for country in ["DE", "ES"]:
    m_c = smf.logit(FORMULA, data=df[df["country"] == country]).fit(disp=0)
    me = m_c.get_margeff(at="overall", dummy=True)
    est[country] = {"coef": (m_c.params["monthly"], m_c.bse["monthly"]),
                    "ame": (100 * me.margeff[0], 100 * me.margeff_se[0])}
for measure in ["coef", "ame"]:
    (b_de, se_de), (b_es, se_es) = est["DE"][measure], est["ES"][measure]
    diff, se = b_es - b_de, np.hypot(se_de, se_es)
    print(f"{measure}: Spain - Germany = {diff:+.3f}, z = {diff / se:+.2f}, "
          f"95 % CI [{diff - 1.96 * se:+.2f}, {diff + 1.96 * se:+.2f}]")
```

How to read it: the coefficients put Germany first (1.189) and Spain last (0.810), a gap of 0.38 that is clearly significant (z about 2.8); the AMEs put Spain first (17.29 pp) and Austria last (12.33 pp), but the Germany–Spain gap of 2.1 pp is within sampling error (z about 0.9). The generator sets the same true effect (1.3) everywhere, but the scale of the unexplained variation is 1.0 in Germany and Austria, 1.5 in Spain and 1.2 in Poland, and a logit coefficient is the true effect divided by the scale: the German lead in coefficients disappears on the probability scale.

## Step 5: satisfaction and response styles

How customers use the 1-to-5 scale, by country:

```{python}
answers = (churn.group_by("country", "satisfaction", maintain_order=True).agg(pl.len().alias("n"))
           .with_columns(share=pl.col("n") / pl.col("n").sum().over("country")))
answer_table = (answers.pivot(on="satisfaction", index="country", values="share", sort_columns=True)
                .join(overview.select("country", "mean_satisfaction"), on="country"))
GT(answer_table).fmt_percent(columns=["1", "2", "3", "4", "5"], decimals=1) \
    .fmt_number(columns="mean_satisfaction", decimals=2) \
    .tab_header(title="Share of answers by satisfaction score", subtitle="Rows add up to 100 %")
```

```{python}
(ggplot(answers.with_columns(pl.col("country").cast(pl.Enum(COUNTRIES))).to_pandas(),
        aes("factor(satisfaction)", "share", fill="country"))
 + geom_col(position=position_dodge(width=0.8), width=0.75)
 + scale_fill_manual(values=COLOURS, breaks=COUNTRIES)
 + scale_y_continuous(labels=percent)
 + labs(x="Satisfaction score", y="Share of answers", fill="")
 + theme_minimal()
 + theme(figure_size=(8, 3.5)))
```

Only 4.0 % of German customers answer 5, but 20.3 % of Spanish customers do; the mean is 2.96 in Germany and 3.35 in Spain. Spanish respondents use the top of the scale more (acquiescence and extreme responding), so the same score does not mean the same satisfaction. Now the separate logits with satisfaction added, once with the raw score and once with the score standardised within each country (a z-score with polars `over("country")`):

```{python}
churn_z = churn.with_columns(
    sat_z=((pl.col("satisfaction") - pl.col("satisfaction").mean())
           / pl.col("satisfaction").std()).over("country"))
df_z = churn_z.to_pandas()

rows = []
for country in COUNTRIES:
    part = df_z[df_z["country"] == country]
    raw = smf.logit(FORMULA + " + satisfaction", data=part).fit(disp=0)
    std = smf.logit(FORMULA + " + sat_z", data=part).fit(disp=0)
    rows.append({"country": country, "sd_satisfaction": part["satisfaction"].std(),
                 "coef_satisfaction": raw.params["satisfaction"], "coef_sat_z": std.params["sat_z"],
                 "coef_monthly": std.params["monthly"]})
GT(pl.DataFrame(rows)).fmt_number(columns="sd_satisfaction", decimals=2) \
    .fmt_number(columns=["coef_satisfaction", "coef_sat_z", "coef_monthly"], decimals=3) \
    .tab_header(title="Satisfaction in separate country logits",
                subtitle="coef_sat_z: per standard deviation within the country")
```

The raw satisfaction coefficient is −0.470 in Germany, −0.557 in Austria, −0.259 in Spain and −0.376 in Poland. Within one country a z-score is only a linear rescaling: the coefficient per standard deviation is the raw coefficient times that country's standard deviation, and the other coefficients (here `monthly`) do not change. The z-score removes differences in the centre and spread of the response style, so "one standard deviation more satisfied" means the same position within each country; it does not remove the logit scale of Step 4, so the coefficients of the countries are still not directly comparable.

How to read it: compare satisfaction across countries only after dealing with response styles (z-scores within country, anchoring vignettes or measurement invariance tests), and still compare effects in percentage points.

## Step 6: interaction and second difference

Does the contract matter more in Spain? The interaction model lets the contract coefficient differ by country.

```{python}
inter = smf.logit("churn ~ monthly * C(country, Treatment('DE')) + price_increase + complaints"
                  " + np.log(tenure_months)", data=df).fit(disp=0)
term = "monthly:C(country, Treatment('DE'))[T.ES]"
ame_inter = ame(inter, df, "monthly")
print(f"product term month-to-month x Spain: {inter.params[term]:.3f} "
      f"(p = {inter.pvalues[term]:.3f})")
print(f"AME of month-to-month: DE {100 * ame_inter['DE']:.2f} pp, "
      f"ES {100 * ame_inter['ES']:.2f} pp; "
      f"second difference {100 * (ame_inter['ES'] - ame_inter['DE']):+.2f} pp")
```

The average predictions behind the chart of slide 35: every customer of a country predicted with `monthly` set to 0 and to 1.

```{python}
avg_pred = pl.DataFrame({
    "country": df["country"].to_list(),
    "pred_24_month": inter.predict(df.assign(monthly=0)).to_list(),
    "pred_month_to_month": inter.predict(df.assign(monthly=1)).to_list(),
}).group_by("country", maintain_order=True).mean()
GT(avg_pred.with_columns(ame_pp=100 * (pl.col("pred_month_to_month") - pl.col("pred_24_month")))) \
    .fmt_percent(columns=["pred_24_month", "pred_month_to_month"], decimals=1) \
    .fmt_number(columns="ame_pp", decimals=2) \
    .tab_header(title="Average predicted churn by contract", subtitle="Interaction model")
```

A 95 % confidence interval for the second difference with the bootstrap: draw customers with replacement within each country, refit, recompute. With 200 resamples this takes a few seconds.

```{python}
def second_difference(data):
    """AME of month-to-month in Spain minus Germany, from the interaction model."""
    fit_b = smf.logit("churn ~ monthly * C(country, Treatment('DE')) + price_increase + complaints"
                      " + np.log(tenure_months)", data=data).fit(disp=0)
    a = ame(fit_b, data, "monthly")
    return a["ES"] - a["DE"]


boot_rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
rows_by_country = [np.flatnonzero(df["country"].to_numpy() == country) for country in COUNTRIES]
draws = []
for _ in range(200):
    idx = np.concatenate([boot_rng.choice(r, size=len(r)) for r in rows_by_country])
    draws.append(second_difference(df.iloc[idx].reset_index(drop=True)))
low, high = 100 * np.percentile(draws, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f"second difference {100 * second_difference(df):+.2f} pp, "
      f"bootstrap 95 % CI [{low:+.2f}, {high:+.2f}] pp")
```

How to read it: the product term is negative (−0.245, p = 0.047) and says "the contract matters less in Spain", but on the probability scale the contract raises churn by 17.93 pp in Spain and 14.16 pp in Germany, a second difference of +3.77 pp; plot, compute the AMEs, compare them, and do not interpret the product term alone (Ai & Norton 2003, Mize 2019). The bootstrap interval of the second difference includes zero, so the data show clearly that the product term misleads about the sign, but only weakly that the contract matters more in Spain.

## Step 7: predictions with confidence intervals and a plotnine curve

The churn probability of a typical profile in each country: month-to-month, a price rise, one complaint call, 12 months of tenure. `get_prediction()` gives the probability with a 95 % confidence interval.

```{python}
profiles = pl.DataFrame({"country": COUNTRIES, "monthly": [1] * 4, "price_increase": [1] * 4,
                         "complaints": [1] * 4, "tenure_months": [12] * 4}).to_pandas()
m.get_prediction(profiles).summary_frame()
```

```{python}
pred = m.get_prediction(profiles).summary_frame()
profile_table = pl.DataFrame({"country": COUNTRIES, "predicted": pred["predicted"].to_list(),
                              "ci_lower": pred["ci_lower"].to_list(),
                              "ci_upper": pred["ci_upper"].to_list()})
GT(profile_table).fmt_number(columns=["predicted", "ci_lower", "ci_upper"], decimals=3) \
    .tab_header(title="Predicted churn probability with 95 % CI",
                subtitle="Month-to-month, price rise, one complaint call, 12 months tenure")
```

The curve a manager understands: predicted churn by tenure for the same profile, per country.

```{python}
grid = pl.DataFrame({"country": np.repeat(COUNTRIES, 60),
                     "tenure_months": np.tile(np.arange(1, 61), 4),
                     "monthly": np.ones(240, dtype=int), "price_increase": np.ones(240, dtype=int),
                     "complaints": np.ones(240, dtype=int)}).to_pandas()
grid = grid.join(m.get_prediction(grid).summary_frame()[["predicted", "ci_lower", "ci_upper"]])

(ggplot(grid, aes("tenure_months", "predicted", color="country", fill="country"))
 + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin="ci_lower", ymax="ci_upper"), alpha=0.15, color=None)
 + geom_line(size=1)
 + scale_color_manual(values=COLOURS, breaks=COUNTRIES)
 + scale_fill_manual(values=COLOURS, breaks=COUNTRIES)
 + scale_y_continuous(labels=percent)
 + labs(x="Tenure (months)", y="Predicted churn probability", color="", fill="",
        title="Month-to-month, price rise, one complaint call")
 + theme_minimal()
 + theme(figure_size=(7, 4)))
```

How to read it: the same customer profile has a churn probability of 35.1 % [32.4, 37.9] in Germany and 60.9 % [58.1, 63.6] in Spain; churn falls with tenure, fastest in the first year.

The pooled model forces one contract slope on all countries, which widens the gap between countries (Step 3). The same profile from the separate country models of Step 4 (country-specific slopes), the numbers on slides 30 and 33:

```{python}
rows = []
for country in COUNTRIES:
    m_c = smf.logit(FORMULA, data=df[df["country"] == country]).fit(disp=0)
    pr = m_c.get_prediction(profiles[profiles["country"] == country]).summary_frame().iloc[0]
    rows.append({"country": country, "predicted": pr["predicted"],
                 "ci_lower": pr["ci_lower"], "ci_upper": pr["ci_upper"]})
GT(pl.DataFrame(rows)).fmt_number(columns=["predicted", "ci_lower", "ci_upper"], decimals=3) \
    .tab_header(title="Predicted churn probability with 95 % CI", subtitle="Separate country models")
```

With country-specific slopes the profile churns at 38.1 % [34.1, 42.2] in Germany and 58.0 % [54.0, 62.0] in Spain: still a large gap, because the Spanish baseline is higher, but narrower than in the pooled model.

## Step 8: train/test split and the confusion matrix

A churn model is judged on customers it has not seen. We fit on a random 70 % of the customers and score the other 30 % (seed 1), with the churn formula plus satisfaction and country dummies.

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
test = rng.random(len(df)) < 0.3
fit = smf.logit(FORMULA + " + satisfaction + C(country)",
                data=df[~test]).fit()
p = fit.predict(df[test]).to_numpy()
y = df.loc[test, "churn"].to_numpy()
print(f"{test.sum():,} test customers, churn rate {y.mean():.3f}")
```

The confusion matrix flags a customer when the predicted churn probability is at or above a threshold. We compare 0.5, 0.3 and the churn rate of the training customers.

```{python}
def confusion(y, p, threshold):
    """Confusion matrix and the usual rates at one threshold."""
    flag = p >= threshold
    tp, fp = (flag & (y == 1)).sum(), (flag & (y == 0)).sum()
    fn, tn = (~flag & (y == 1)).sum(), (~flag & (y == 0)).sum()
    return {"threshold": float(threshold),
            "TP": int(tp), "FP": int(fp), "FN": int(fn), "TN": int(tn),
            "accuracy": (tp + tn) / len(y), "recall": tp / (tp + fn),
            "precision": tp / (tp + fp), "share_flagged": flag.mean()}


base_rate = df.loc[~test, "churn"].mean()
thresholds = pl.DataFrame([confusion(y, p, t) for t in [0.5, 0.3, base_rate]])
print(f"accuracy of 'nobody churns': {1 - y.mean():.3f}")
GT(thresholds).fmt_number(columns="threshold", decimals=3) \
    .fmt_integer(columns=["TP", "FP", "FN", "TN"]) \
    .fmt_number(columns=["accuracy", "recall", "precision", "share_flagged"], decimals=3) \
    .tab_header(title="Confusion matrix on the test customers",
                subtitle="Third row: threshold = churn rate of the training customers")
```

At 0.5 the model flags 8.6 % of the customers and catches 22 % of the churners (recall 0.220, precision 0.623); its accuracy of 0.779 is barely above the 0.758 of predicting "nobody churns". Lower thresholds catch more churners at the price of more false alarms; the right threshold follows from the costs (Step 11). A random split is the minimum: a churn model is used next quarter, so out-of-time validation (fit on earlier months, score later ones) is better practice. These data have no snapshot months, so we use the random split.

How to read it: accuracy is the wrong yardstick for churn; look at recall, precision and the share flagged at the threshold you would use.

## Step 9: AUC, Gini, top-decile lift and gains chart

Ranking quality without a threshold. The AUC is the probability that a random churner gets a higher predicted probability than a random stayer; the rank formula (Mann-Whitney) computes it in three lines.

```{python}
def lift_auc(y, p, top=0.1):
    """Top-decile lift and AUC (rank formula)."""
    order = np.argsort(-p)
    k = int(round(top * len(y)))
    lift = y[order[:k]].mean() / y.mean()
    ranks = pl.Series(p).rank().to_numpy()
    n1 = y.sum()
    auc = (ranks[y == 1].sum() - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * (len(y) - n1))
    return lift, auc


lift, auc = lift_auc(y, p)
print(f"AUC {auc:.3f}, Gini {2 * auc - 1:.3f}, top-decile lift {lift:.2f}")
```

Top-decile lift in two lines, as on slide 46: the churn rate among the 10 % of customers with the highest predicted probability, divided by the overall churn rate.

```{python}
top = np.argsort(-p)[:round(0.1 * len(y))]
lift = y[top].mean() / y.mean()          # 2.46
# ties: two customers share the predicted probability at the cut; another sort order (e.g. kind="stable")
# can swap them and move the lift in the second decimal (2.47)
print(f"{len(top)} customers in the top decile: churn {y[top].mean():.3f} vs {y.mean():.3f} "
      f"overall, lift {lift:.2f}")
```

The decile table: customers ranked by predicted churn, decile 1 = highest risk. Decile 1 holds the same 328 customers as `top`.

```{python}
order = np.argsort(-p)                    # same order as top, also for tied predictions
ranked = (pl.DataFrame({"p": p[order], "churn": y[order]})
          .with_columns(decile=(pl.int_range(1, pl.len() + 1) * 10 / pl.len())
                        .ceil().cast(pl.Int64)))
deciles = (ranked.group_by("decile").agg(pl.len().alias("customers"),
                                         pl.col("churn").sum().alias("churners"),
                                         pl.col("churn").mean().alias("churn_rate"),
                                         pl.col("p").mean().alias("mean_predicted"))
           .sort("decile")
           .with_columns(lift=pl.col("churn_rate") / y.mean(),
                         cum_gain=pl.col("churners").cum_sum() / pl.col("churners").sum()))
GT(deciles).fmt_number(columns=["churn_rate", "mean_predicted", "cum_gain"], decimals=3) \
    .fmt_number(columns="lift", decimals=2).tab_header(title="Deciles of predicted churn")
```

The cumulative gains chart: the share of all churners reached when contacting the top x % of customers.

```{python}
n = len(y)
gains = pl.DataFrame({"share_contacted": np.arange(0, n + 1) / n,
                      "share_churners": np.r_[0, np.cumsum(y[order])] / y.sum()})
marks = gains.filter(pl.col("share_contacted").is_in(
    [round(s * n) / n for s in [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5]]))
print(marks)

(ggplot(gains.to_pandas(), aes("share_contacted", "share_churners"))
 + geom_abline(linetype="dashed", color="#8C8C8C")
 + geom_line(color="#002350", size=1)
 + geom_point(marks.to_pandas(), color="#0096D3", size=3)
 + scale_x_continuous(labels=percent)
 + scale_y_continuous(labels=percent)
 + labs(x="Share of customers contacted (ranked by predicted churn)",
        y="Share of churners reached", title="Cumulative gains on the test customers")
 + theme_minimal()
 + theme(figure_size=(6, 4.5)))
```

How to read it: AUC 0.764 (Gini 0.529); calling the top 10 % reaches 24.6 % of all churners (59.5 % of them churn, a lift of 2.46), the top 30 % reaches 57.3 % and the top half 78.8 %.

## Step 10: calibration

Does a predicted 30 % mean that about 30 % churn? The Brier score is the mean squared error of the predicted probabilities; the reference is the score of predicting the churn rate for everyone, ȳ(1 − ȳ).

```{python}
brier = np.mean((p - y) ** 2)
print(f"Brier score {brier:.3f}; "
      f"predicting the churn rate for everyone: {y.mean() * (1 - y.mean()):.3f}")

calibration = (pl.DataFrame({"p": p, "churn": y})
               .with_columns(bin=pl.col("p").qcut(10, labels=[str(i) for i in range(1, 11)]))
               .group_by("bin").agg(pl.col("p").mean().alias("mean_predicted"),
                                    pl.col("churn").mean().alias("observed"),
                                    pl.len().alias("customers"))
               .sort("mean_predicted"))
GT(calibration).fmt_number(columns=["mean_predicted", "observed"], decimals=3) \
    .tab_header(title="Calibration by decile of predicted churn")
```

```{python}
(ggplot(calibration.to_pandas(), aes("mean_predicted", "observed"))
 + geom_abline(linetype="dashed", color="#8C8C8C")
 + geom_line(color="#002350")
 + geom_point(color="#002350", size=2.5)
 + scale_x_continuous(labels=percent, limits=(0, 0.7))
 + scale_y_continuous(labels=percent, limits=(0, 0.7))
 + labs(x="Mean predicted churn (decile)", y="Observed churn")
 + theme_minimal()
 + theme(figure_size=(4.5, 4.5)))
```

Two summary numbers: the calibration slope (a logit of churn on the log-odds of the prediction; ideal 1) and calibration-in-the-large (the intercept when the log-odds of the prediction enter as an offset; ideal 0).

```{python}
lp = np.log(p / (1 - p))                                     # predicted log-odds
slope = sm.Logit(y, sm.add_constant(lp)).fit(disp=0).params[1]
citl = sm.GLM(y, np.ones_like(lp), family=sm.families.Binomial(), offset=lp).fit().params[0]
print(f"calibration slope {slope:.3f}, calibration-in-the-large {citl:.3f}")
```

A note on oversampling. Churners are a minority, and some analysts sample 50/50 before fitting. For a logit this leaves the slopes and the AUC almost unchanged but shifts the intercept, so every predicted probability is too high and the calibration of this step breaks. If you sample on the outcome, correct the intercept afterwards (King & Zeng 2001): $\hat\beta_0^{\text{corrected}} = \hat\beta_0 - \ln\left[\frac{1 - \tau}{\tau} \cdot \frac{\bar y}{1 - \bar y}\right]$, where τ is the churn rate in the population and ȳ the churn share in the sample.

How to read it: the predictions are well calibrated on these test customers (Brier 0.152 vs 0.183, slope 1.06, calibration-in-the-large 0.06), because test and training customers come from the same period and countries; Step 13 shows a case where they are not.

## Step 11: campaign profit and the cost threshold

What is the best number of customers to contact? The economics are invented for teaching: a customer who stays is worth LTV = EUR 400, a share γ = 0.25 of the contacted would-be churners accepts the offer and stays, the offer costs δ = EUR 30 (paid by every contacted customer who takes it) and each contact c = EUR 3. With customers ranked by predicted churn, the profit of contacting the top k is (Neslin et al. 2006)

profit_k = (γ·LTV + δ·(1 − γ)) · churners among the top k − (δ + c) · k.

```{python}
LTV, gamma, delta, contact_cost = 400, 0.25, 30, 3          # EUR, illustrative
cum_churners = np.cumsum(y[order])                     # order of Step 9
k = np.arange(1, n + 1)
profit = (gamma * LTV + delta * (1 - gamma)) * cum_churners - (delta + contact_cost) * k
best = profit.argmax()
p_star = (contact_cost + delta) / (gamma * LTV + delta * (1 - gamma))
print(f"optimum: contact the top {k[best] / n:.3f} of customers, profit EUR {profit[best]:,.0f}")
print(f"top 10 %: EUR {profit[round(0.1 * n) - 1]:,.0f}; everyone: EUR {profit[-1]:,.0f}")
print(f"break-even churn probability p* = {p_star:.3f}; share above p*: {(p > p_star).mean():.3f}")
```

```{python}
profit_curve = pl.DataFrame({"share_contacted": k / n, "profit": profit / 1000})
(ggplot(profit_curve.to_pandas(), aes("share_contacted", "profit"))
 + geom_hline(yintercept=0, color="#8C8C8C")
 + geom_line(color="#002350", size=1)
 + geom_point(pl.DataFrame({"share_contacted": [k[best] / n],
                            "profit": [profit[best] / 1000]}).to_pandas(), color="#0096D3", size=3)
 + scale_x_continuous(labels=percent)
 + labs(x="Share of customers contacted (ranked by predicted churn)",
        y="Campaign profit (EUR thousand)", title="Illustrative campaign economics")
 + theme_minimal()
 + theme(figure_size=(6, 4)))
```

How to read it: profit peaks when the top 39 % are contacted (EUR 25,262 on these 3,284 customers) and turns negative when everyone gets the offer (EUR −11,107); the per-customer rule "contact if p > p* = 0.27" gives a similar depth (33 % of customers) but needs calibrated probabilities (Step 10).

## Step 12: uplift with the randomised offer

High churn risk is not the same as a large response to the offer. Because the offer was assigned at random, the difference in churn between customers with and without the offer is its effect, in any group we form before the offer. First a risk score: a churn model fitted only on the customers without the offer, so the offer does not contaminate the score, then quartiles of that score for all customers.

```{python}
ctrl = df[df["retention_offer"] == 0]
risk = smf.logit(FORMULA + " + satisfaction + C(country)",
                 data=ctrl).fit().predict(df)
df["risk"] = risk
df["risk_group"] = pl.Series(df["risk"]).qcut(
    4, labels=["Q1 low", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4 high"]).to_list()
df.pivot_table("churn", "risk_group", "retention_offer")
```

Churn without (0) and with (1) the offer in each risk quartile: the code of slide 46. The table below adds the difference with its confidence interval.

The offer effect per group, with a 95 % confidence interval for the difference of two proportions:

```{python}
def offer_effect(data, group):
    """Churn without and with the offer, the difference in pp and its 95 % CI, by group."""
    offer = pl.col("retention_offer")
    return (data.group_by(group).agg(
                pl.len().alias("n"),
                (offer == 0).sum().alias("n0"), (offer == 1).sum().alias("n1"),
                pl.col("churn").filter(offer == 0).mean().alias("without"),
                pl.col("churn").filter(offer == 1).mean().alias("with_offer"))
            .with_columns(effect_pp=100 * (pl.col("with_offer") - pl.col("without")),
                          se_pp=100 * (pl.col("without") * (1 - pl.col("without")) / pl.col("n0")
                                       + pl.col("with_offer") * (1 - pl.col("with_offer"))
                                       / pl.col("n1")).sqrt())
            .with_columns(low_pp=pl.col("effect_pp") - 1.96 * pl.col("se_pp"),
                          high_pp=pl.col("effect_pp") + 1.96 * pl.col("se_pp"))
            .rename({group: "group"})
            .with_columns(pl.col("group").cast(pl.String))
            .sort("group")
            .drop("se_pp"))


pilot = pl.from_pandas(df).with_columns(
    complaint_group=pl.when(pl.col("complaints") >= 3).then(pl.lit("3+"))
    .otherwise(pl.col("complaints").cast(pl.String)))
by_risk = offer_effect(pilot, "risk_group")
by_complaints = offer_effect(pilot, "complaint_group")
effects = pl.concat([by_risk.with_columns(split=pl.lit("By predicted churn risk (quartile)")),
                     by_complaints.with_columns(split=pl.lit("By complaint calls"))])
GT(effects, groupname_col="split", rowname_col="group") \
    .fmt_integer(columns=["n", "n0", "n1"]).fmt_number(columns=["without", "with_offer"], decimals=3) \
    .fmt_number(columns=["effect_pp", "low_pp", "high_pp"], decimals=1, force_sign=True) \
    .tab_header(title="Effect of the retention offer on churn",
                subtitle="Randomised pilot; negative = fewer churners")
```

An uplift model lets the offer effect depend on complaints and the contract. The predicted uplift of a customer is the predicted churn with the offer minus without it.

```{python}
two = smf.logit("churn ~ retention_offer * (complaints + monthly) + price_increase"
                " + np.log(tenure_months) + C(country)", data=df).fit(disp=0)
uplift = two.predict(df.assign(retention_offer=1)) - two.predict(df.assign(retention_offer=0))
print(f"mean predicted uplift {100 * uplift.mean():+.2f} pp; "
      f"correlation of risk and uplift {np.corrcoef(df['risk'], uplift)[0, 1]:.2f}")
```

The correlation is negative because uplift is negative when the offer helps: on average, customers with a higher risk get a larger reduction, but far from one to one.

```{python}
panels = pl.Enum(["By predicted churn risk (quartile)", "By complaint calls"])
effects_plot = effects.with_columns(
    colour=pl.when(pl.col("group") == "3+").then(pl.lit("grey")).otherwise(pl.lit("blue")),
    split=pl.col("split").cast(panels))
(ggplot(effects_plot.to_pandas(), aes("group", "effect_pp", fill="colour"))
 + geom_hline(yintercept=0, color="#8C8C8C")
 + geom_col(width=0.65)
 + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin="low_pp", ymax="high_pp"), width=0.2)
 + facet_wrap("~split", scales="free_x")
 + scale_fill_manual(values={"blue": "#0096D3", "grey": "#8C8C8C"}, guide=None)
 + labs(x="", y="Offer effect on churn (pp)")
 + theme_minimal()
 + theme(figure_size=(8, 3.8)))
```

How to read it: the offer lowers churn by 3.3 pp in the lowest risk quartile, by 11.1 pp in the third and by 10.2 pp in the highest, and from three complaint calls on it does not help (+8.2 pp on 377 customers, with a confidence interval that includes zero); the highest-risk customers are not the ones the offer moves most, so target uplift, not risk, which needs a randomised control group (Ascarza 2018).

## Step 13: does the model travel?

A model fitted on German customers, used in the other countries. We fit the churn formula with satisfaction on the German training customers, score the test customers of every country and compare with each country's own model, fitted on its own training customers.

```{python}
de_model = smf.logit(FORMULA + " + satisfaction",
                     data=df[~test & (df["country"] == "DE")]).fit(disp=0)

rows = []
for country in COUNTRIES:
    in_country = (df["country"] == country).to_numpy()
    own = smf.logit(FORMULA + " + satisfaction", data=df[~test & in_country]).fit(disp=0)
    scored = df[test & in_country]
    y_c = scored["churn"].to_numpy()
    p_de, p_own = de_model.predict(scored).to_numpy(), own.predict(scored).to_numpy()
    rows.append({"country": country, "auc_german_model": lift_auc(y_c, p_de)[1],
                 "auc_own_model": lift_auc(y_c, p_own)[1],
                 "mean_pred_german_model": p_de.mean(), "actual_churn": y_c.mean()})
transfer = pl.DataFrame(rows)
GT(transfer).fmt_number(columns=["auc_german_model", "auc_own_model", "mean_pred_german_model",
                                 "actual_churn"], decimals=3) \
    .tab_header(title="German model vs own model, test customers")
```

The German model ranks Spanish customers almost as well as Spain's own model (AUC 0.709 vs 0.718), but predicts 15.7 % churn where 35.2 % churn. The fix is to recalibrate the intercept on local data: keep the German coefficients as an offset (the German linear predictor) and estimate only a constant on the Spanish training customers.

```{python}
es_train = df[~test & (df["country"] == "ES")]
es_test = df[test & (df["country"] == "ES")]
shift = smf.glm("churn ~ 1", data=es_train, family=sm.families.Binomial(),
                offset=de_model.predict(es_train, which="linear")).fit().params["Intercept"]
recalibrated = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(de_model.predict(es_test, which="linear") + shift)))
print(f"intercept shift for Spain: {shift:+.3f}")
print(f"mean predicted churn in Spain: German model {de_model.predict(es_test).mean():.3f}, "
      f"recalibrated {recalibrated.mean():.3f}, actual {es_test['churn'].mean():.3f}")
auc_recal = lift_auc(es_test["churn"].to_numpy(), recalibrated.to_numpy())[1]
print(f"AUC after recalibration: {auc_recal:.3f}")
```

How to read it: the ranking travels, the level does not; shifting the intercept moves the mean prediction to the Spanish level and leaves the AUC unchanged, because a common shift in log-odds does not change the order of the customers.
